title: Partition Labels
statement: Given a string s of lowercase letters, partition it into as many parts as possible so that each letter appears in at most one part. The parts, concatenated in order, must reproduce s. Return a list of the part sizes.
realWorld: Splitting a stream of events into independent batches so that no key crosses a batch boundary — then each batch can be shipped to a different worker with no coordination. The same computation is how a compiler decides where a variable's live range ends, and how a log compactor finds safe cut points.

examples.explanation: The first part is "ababcbaca": it must run to index 8 because that is the last 'a', even though 'b' and 'c' were finished earlier. Cutting anywhere before index 8 would put an 'a' in two parts.
The last 'c' is at index 9 and the first is at index 1, so the very first part is forced to swallow the entire string. The maximum number of parts can be one.
No letter repeats, so every position is a legal cut and the greedy takes all of them. The sizes always sum to s.length(), which is the cheapest check on any solution here.

constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters only
Parts must appear in the same order as in s

bruteForce.idea: For each candidate cut point, verify it: collect the set of letters to its left and the set to its right and check they are disjoint. Cut at the first position where they are, then repeat on the remainder.
code: for (int i = start; i <= cut; i++) left.add(s.charAt(i));
for (int i = cut + 1; i < s.length(); i++) {

complexity.space: O(1) — at most 26 letters in the set

bruteForce.whySlow: Every candidate cut re-scans the entire suffix to ask 'does any letter behind me appear again ahead?'. That question is settled by one number per letter — the index of its last occurrence — and there are only 26 such numbers. The inner scan recomputes last-occurrence information from scratch at every one of the n positions, throwing away the identical information it computed at the previous position.

patternIdentification: A part can end no earlier than the last occurrence of every letter it contains — each letter inside it is a commitment to reach at least that far. So precompute each letter's last index once, carry a running maximum of those commitments as you scan, and close the part exactly when the scan index catches the running maximum: at that moment nothing inside reaches past you. Greedy is safe because closing at the earliest legal point can never cost you parts — any other valid partition's first boundary lies at or after this one, and cutting earlier leaves a longer remaining suffix, which can only be split into at least as many parts. Whenever a segment's validity is decided by a 'furthest commitment' of the items inside it, this is the shape: precompute the commitment, scan with a running maximum, close on equality.

optimized.idea: One pass to record last[c], the final index of each letter. Then one pass with two variables: start, where the current part began, and end, the furthest index anything in the current part is committed to. At each index, extend end by the current letter's last occurrence; when i equals end, close the part and reset start.
code: for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) last[s.charAt(i) - 'a'] = i;   // last write wins = last occurrence

commonMistakes: Recording the *first* occurrence of each letter instead of the last (guarding the write with 'if not already seen'). Every commitment then points backwards, i == end fires almost immediately, and "ababcbacadefegdehijhklij" comes back as twelve ragged parts starting [1, 1, 3, 5, ...] instead of [9, 7, 8].

Closing the part when `i == last[s.charAt(i) - 'a']` — that cuts at the last occurrence of the *current* letter rather than of every letter seen so far. The same input cuts after index 5, where the last 'b' sits, producing a first part of 6 while an 'a' and a 'c' are still to come.

Computing the size as `end - start` instead of `i - start + 1`, or forgetting to reset start. Each part comes out one short and [9,7,8] becomes [8,6,7]; the sizes no longer add up to s.length(), which is the one-line assertion that catches this class of bug immediately.
